title: Jean-François Lyotard
tradition: Poststructuralism: the postmodern and the differend
keyWorks: Answering the Question: What Is Postmodernism? (1982)
Lessons on the Analytic of the Sublime (1991)
summary: Jean-François Lyotard was a French philosopher who brought the word “postmodern” into wide use. He described our age as a time of “incredulity toward metanarratives” — the grand stories, like “progress will fix everything,” that once explained the meaning of it all. He was drawn to whatever doesn’t fit into a shared language: injustice that cannot be voiced, and “the sublime” — an experience that exceeds any picture of it.
onEmotions: For Lyotard, a feeling is often the first sign that something is happening for which we don’t yet have words. In The Differend he writes that when something must be put into words but cannot yet be, a feeling signals it — and that feeling deserves respect, not to be drowned out with ready-made formulas. In Libidinal Economy he insisted that affects are “intensities,” energy that can never be fully translated into rational theories. And his reflections on “the sublime” describe a mixture of pain and pleasure before something greater than us. Lyotard helps you treat your feelings as witnesses, not as mistakes.

anxiety.text: “Is it happening?” — for Lyotard, the central question of the sublime and of every beginning. When anxiety catches you waiting — what if something happens, or nothing ever happens again — it asks the same thing, minus the elation. In thinking about “the sublime,” Lyotard drew on Edmund Burke, who wrote that the deepest terror is the terror of privation: of light, of other people, of language. Lyotard carries this thought over to time: what unsettles us is not so much the event itself as the not-knowing — whether anything will come next. The question “Is it happening?” hangs in the air. But for Lyotard that same uncertainty is also a source of openness: the future is not written in advance, so something new is possible in it. From Lyotard’s point of view, anxiety can be understood as a heightened sense of time — a sensitivity to the fact that life is unfinished. That is hard to bear, but there is something alive in it too.
anxiety.practice: Put your palm on your chest and with each heartbeat note to yourself: “it is happening.” For a minute, just notice that life is already going on — right now.

fear.text: As a young man Lyotard seriously considered becoming a monk or a painter — and perhaps that is why he looked so closely at the feeling where fear is mixed with elation. Your fear is a strong and entirely legitimate feeling: it tells you that something before you is bigger than you. Following Kant and Burke, Lyotard thought a great deal about “the sublime” — a mixed feeling that holds both fear and a strange pleasure. We feel it before a storm, mountains, the night sky — before whatever won’t fit into our imagination. Burke had already noticed that the sublime arises when the threat is held at a distance: we still sense its power, but we are no longer crushed by it. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that not every fear has to be conquered. Sometimes it is enough to find a distance at which it turns into a sense of scale — the understanding that you have touched something greater, and are still here.
fear.practice: Go out in the evening and look at the sky or at something very large — clouds, buildings, trees — for a minute. Let fear sit next to wonder, without choosing between them.

sadness.text: Libidinal Economy, his boldest book, Lyotard later called his “evil book” — in it he revolted against the habit of immediately translating feelings into theory, diagnosis or morals. Your sadness doesn’t have to have an explanation or a use. He described affects as “intensities” — clots of energy that pass through us and can never be reduced to meaning without remainder. Trying to explain an intensity at once often muffles it. It follows that your sadness doesn’t need to pass a reasonableness test. It isn’t necessarily “about something” or “for something.” You can let it simply be an intensity — feel its weight and its colour, without forcing yourself to find a cause, a lesson or a way out right away.
sadness.practice: Sit with the sadness for five minutes without explaining it to yourself or anyone. Just notice where it is felt in your body and how its “intensity” shifts.

grief.text: Lyotard would begin with silence — not an empty one, but a full one. In grief, perhaps the hardest of feelings to put into words, it is entirely natural that words fall short, and in The Differend he describes exactly such states: something must be said, but the existing language won’t do. He stresses that even silence is a “phrase” — something is being said in it too — and that the signal of such a state is a feeling. Pain, for Lyotard, is a sign that new words need to be sought, rather than rushing to ready-made consolations like “time heals.” In other words, your grief doesn’t have to fit accepted formulas, and its silence is meaningful. The little word “yet” in his definition matters too: what cannot be expressed now may, in time, find its form.
grief.practice: Spend a minute in silence dedicated to the one or the thing you lost. Let that silence be your phrase — it speaks too.

quote.text: The differend is the unstable state and instant of language wherein something which must be able to be put into phrases cannot yet be.
quote.author: Jean-François Lyotard

loneliness.text: A joke answered in earnest, a request taken as a reproach — Lyotard would call this a meeting of different “language games.” Loneliness can be especially sharp when no one seems to hear you: you speak, and your words fly past. Lyotard explained this through the idea of “language games” (a notion he borrowed from Wittgenstein): people speak in different modes — reasoning, asking, complaining, joking — and these modes don’t always translate into one another. What carries weight in your “language” may simply have no weight in someone else’s. Lyotard might say that loneliness is not always the absence of people but the absence of a shared game in which someone picks up your phrase. Lyotard believed in “little narratives” — small communities with their own stories. The task is not to be understood by everyone, but to find those who speak a language close to yours.
loneliness.practice: Today, say one sentence to someone in a different “genre” than usual: not a complaint but a question, not advice but a joke. Notice whether it gets picked up.

anger.text: There are disputes for which no court exists anywhere — Lyotard devoted a whole book, The Differend, to them. Your anger, flaring up at injustice, deserves to be taken seriously, and his distinction between two kinds of conflict helps here. A “litigation” is a dispute that can be settled by shared rules, as in a court. A “differend” (le différend) is a conflict where there are no rules acceptable to both sides, and one side cannot even voice its wrong in the other’s language. A victim, for Lyotard, is someone deprived of the means to prove the damage done to them. So your anger may be the signal of a differend: you were harmed, but there is no “court” where this will be recognised. Then anger is not a whim but a testimony. Lyotard urged us not to silence such feelings but to look for new words and new listeners able to receive them.
anger.practice: Say aloud, briefly and calmly, what exactly the injustice is — as if an honest judge were listening. Then think who in your life could be such a listener.

shame.text: “Does it work?” — Lyotard noticed that the modern world asks this question not only of machines but of people too. Shame, the feeling in which you want to become invisible, often answers it on your behalf. In The Postmodern Condition, Lyotard described how the modern world increasingly values “performativity” — efficiency, a favourable ratio of input to output. Knowledge, work, and people along with them are judged by how well they “perform” in the system. Lyotard noticed a hidden pressure behind this criterion: whoever doesn’t measure up is simply no longer let into the game. Lyotard would probably note that much of today’s shame is not shame over a bad deed but over “insufficient efficiency.” Yet performativity is only one language among many, not the measure of human worth. Your life is also made of “games” where efficiency means nothing: friendship, care, contemplation.
shame.practice: Do one completely inefficient thing today — slowly, with pleasure and no result: watch a cloud, stroke a cat, reread a favourite line.

guilt.text: Imagine a poem judged by the laws of bookkeeping — Lyotard would call that an injustice between “genres.” Your guilt is a sign that you feel responsible, and that is an important, worthy feeling. In The Differend, Lyotard stressed that there are different “genres” of discourse — cognitive, economic, ethical — and each has its own tribunal. Injustice arises when one genre judges what belongs to another: for example, when a relationship is assessed like a deal, or rest like work. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that it helps to ask which “tribunal” is passing sentence on you. Sometimes guilt is fair: you really did hurt someone, and that can be acknowledged and made right. But sometimes you are being judged by the wrong genre — for instance, by the logic of productivity where you were simply being human. Then guilt is a mistake of jurisdiction, not the truth about you.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself aloud: “Which court is judging me right now — conscience, work, other people’s expectations?” If it isn’t the court of conscience, tell it: “You are not my tribunal.”

envy.text: How do you compare a sonnet with a marathon? Lyotard would answer: you can’t — they share no common measure. Envy is painful, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. But it’s worth noticing: envy assumes a single common scale on which your life and someone else’s can be compared. Lyotard argued against such scales all his life. In The Postmodern Condition he describes our time as an age of incredulity toward “metanarratives” — grand stories that explain where everyone should be heading and what counts as success. And in The Differend he insists on incommensurability: different lives and different “language games” cannot be converted into common points without loss. It follows that envy is the moment you believed in a single ladder on which someone stands higher. But if there are many ladders, the comparison loses its force, and your path is not falling behind — it is a different game.
envy.practice: Name three “games” your life is played in — friendship, a craft, some small skill. Ask: by the rules of which one are you comparing yourself right now?

emptiness.text: The smallest soul there could possibly be — that is what Lyotard wrote one of his late essays about. Emptiness and apathy, when nothing inside responds, can be very heavy, and this thought may help. In his late essay “Anima Minima” (from the collection Postmodern Fables), Lyotard offers a simple and profound thought: the soul exists when something touches it. A sound, a colour, a touch awakens it; without such contacts it seems to fall asleep. Lyotard sees this not as a verdict but as a description of how fragile and sensuous our make-up is. In other words, emptiness is not proof that there is nothing inside, but a state in which the soul is waiting for a sensation. You don’t need to demand strong feelings from yourself. Something very small is enough — a single sound, a single shade that touches you even a little.
emptiness.practice: Hold your hands under a stream of cool water for a minute, doing nothing, only feeling. Give your “minimal soul” one clear touch.

confusion.text: In 1985 Lyotard curated an exhibition at the Centre Pompidou, Les Immatériaux: visitors wandered through half-lit rooms wearing headphones, and no route was the “right” one. Feeling lost is natural in a world with no single story that explains everything. This is exactly what Lyotard called “the postmodern condition.” People used to be held up by “metanarratives” — grand stories of progress, emancipation and truth that gave meaning to every individual life. Today they are believed less and less, and what remains is a multitude of “little narratives” that don’t add up to a single picture. Lyotard didn’t mourn this: he saw instability as a source of inventiveness — what he called “paralogy,” the search for the new through dissent and paradox. From Lyotard’s point of view, your confusion is not a malfunction but an honest experience of the age. You don’t have to wait for a final story; you can assemble your own from small fragments tested by experience.
confusion.practice: Walk for five minutes without a route: at each corner, turn wherever you feel drawn. Notice that you can walk without an overall map.

quote.text: Simplifying to the extreme, I define postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives.
quote.author: Jean-François Lyotard

fatigue.text: The endless conveyor of “more, faster, more efficient” Lyotard called not progress but “the inhuman.” Your tiredness and burnout are not a personal flaw. As early as 1979, Lyotard described “performativity” as the main criterion of modern society: maximum output for minimum input. In The Inhuman he went further: “development” behaves like an inhuman process that uses people as a resource and demands ever more speed and efficiency. It seems that your tiredness is a differend between your body and the logic of endless optimisation. The body speaks its own language, one the system doesn’t know how to hear. To acknowledge your tiredness is to give a voice to the side that usually goes unheard. Rest, in this sense, is not a whim but the restoration of justice toward yourself.
fatigue.practice: Choose one task today and do it twice as slowly as usual — on purpose, as a small strike against acceleration.

boredom.text: A drop about to fall from a tap — Lyotard could have watched such a small “now” for a long time. Boredom is the feeling that nothing is happening, and it can be genuinely oppressive. Lyotard was deeply preoccupied with the very fact of the event — that something happens rather than nothing. In an essay on the painter Barnett Newman he writes about the “now” — the instant in which something occurs before we have understood what it is. The question “Is it happening?” is central to his understanding of the sublime. Lyotard would probably note that boredom arises when we expect events only in their familiar, anticipated form. But even in the emptiest minute something is happening: the light shifts, a sound rises and fades. Boredom can become a threshold of attention — a place where you learn to notice the barely perceptible “now.”
boredom.practice: For a minute, watch something about to change: a drop on the tap, a cloud, a candle flame. Catch the instant when “it happens.”

joy.text: Lyotard argued with those who demand a pass from every feeling — usefulness, meaning, moral justification. Your joy needs no such pass. In Libidinal Economy Lyotard defended affects as “intensities” that can never be fully subordinated to reason, system or morality. Later, in the essay “Anima Minima,” he wrote that the soul lives by what touches it: colour, sound, touch. Joy, in this light, is an especially pure example of such an intensity: it happens as an event and doesn’t need to fit into some grand success story. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that don’t turn joy into proof that “everything is going right.” It is not a result but an occurrence. You can simply accept it — the way you accept a day that has suddenly turned warm.
joy.practice: Choose one small thing that delights you — a taste, a tune, warm light — and for a minute simply let it “touch” you, extracting nothing from it.

love.text: Two people can live together for forty years and still find untranslated words in each other — Lyotard would see in this not a failure but a small miracle. Love and tenderness are living, beautiful feelings, and a subtle thought about them follows from his ideas. He insisted that each of us has our own “language games” and our own “idiom” — a way of speaking and feeling that can never be fully translated into someone else’s language. It follows that to love is to meet someone who will never be fully translatable into your language, and not to demand that they be. A love that respects the untranslatability of the other doesn’t try to reduce them to a “common denominator.” And his defence of “intensities” is a reminder: tenderness doesn’t have to be explained or justified. It simply happens between two different people.
love.practice: Ask someone close about a word or phrase they love, and ask them to explain what it means to them. Listen to their “idiom” without correcting it.

gratitude.text: Why is there something rather than nothing? Lyotard turned this old question of Leibniz into an everyday wonder: here is a phrase, here a meeting, here a morning — and they might not have been. Gratitude is the feeling that something was given to you rather than earned. Reflecting on the sublime, he stresses that the fact that anything occurs at all — a phrase, a meeting, a moment — is not guaranteed and not produced to plan. In other words, gratitude is the recognition of an event as a gift. It doesn’t need to be squeezed into the logic of exchange, “I give to you, you give to me”: in a world of performativity everything is measured by results, while gratitude sees what no calculation can capture. By noticing what came to you without merit and without a plan, you step out of endless accountability and accept life as an event.
gratitude.practice: In the evening, name aloud three events of the day that might not have happened: a conversation, light in a window, someone’s smile. Say to each: “Thank you for happening.”

hope.text: Kant looked for a sign of a better future not in the French Revolution itself but in the enthusiasm of distant onlookers who sympathised with it — Lyotard devoted a whole book to this. Hope can seem out of place when the grand stories about a bright future no longer convince. Lyotard did indeed think that the age of “metanarratives” was over. But he was no pessimist. First, for him the future is fundamentally open: the event is unpredictable, and that is its strength. Second, instead of one great story we have many “little narratives” — local, alive, our own. Lyotard might say that hope doesn’t need a guarantee of universal progress. It can rest on small things — on the next step, on a single meeting, on the chance that tomorrow something may happen that you can’t yet even imagine. Such hope is humbler, but it is harder to disappoint.
hope.practice: Find one small “sign of history” today — a stranger’s act that moved you. Tell someone about it.

nostalgia.text: The Postmodern Explained to Children — Lyotard gave this title to a collection of letters, and much in them is about how to live once the old grand stories are gone. Nostalgia is a longing for what has been lost, and there is much tenderness in it. Lyotard wrote about nostalgia on a historical scale: a longing for the grand stories that once gave life a clear meaning — faith in progress, in a single truth, in a shared “we.” He noted that many people have lost even this nostalgia — and added at once that this by no means turns them into barbarians: meaning doesn’t vanish, it passes into little stories and everyday practices. It seems that personal nostalgia can also be a longing for a whole story in which everything made sense. You can honour it without trying to bring back the past in its entirety. What was valuable lives on in fragments — in habits, words, people.
nostalgia.practice: Tell someone one small story from the past — not “how things were better,” but one concrete scene with a smell and a sound. A little narrative lives as long as it is told.

quote.text: Most people have lost the nostalgia for the lost narrative.
quote.author: Jean-François Lyotard

craving.text: “To link is necessary; how to link is not” — this formula of Lyotard’s sounds dry until a craving arrives. An acute “I want it right now” feels like an order you cannot help but obey, and that is genuinely hard. In The Differend, Lyotard describes life as a chain of “phrases” — not only words but gestures, glances, actions. One of his key thoughts: after every phrase there will necessarily be a next one, but what it will be is not decided in advance. Linking is inevitable; how to link is open. Lyotard would probably note that a craving is a strong phrase that insists on a single continuation. But it is only one possible response, not a law. Between the wave of desire and the action there is a moment when you can “link” differently: a sip of water, a phone call, five steps across the room. The wave of craving rises and falls, and the next phrase is still yours.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, name to yourself three other possible “next steps” — any at all, even strange ones. Choose one and do it.

addiction.text: One minister seizing every ministry — friendship, sleep, play: Lyotard would call this the hegemony of one genre. When life has been built around one thing for years — a substance, gambling, a screen — breaking out of the circle is very hard, and it is not a moral failure. In The Differend, Lyotard describes different “genres of discourse” — knowledge, friendship, play, care, dreaming — each with its own aims and rules. Injustice, for Lyotard, arises when one genre seizes power over all the others and begins to subordinate them to its own aim. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that addiction resembles such a hegemony — one aim gradually rebuilds everything around itself: time, relationships, money, thoughts. Recovery, then, is not a single heroic act of will but a slow return of voice to the other genres of life. And here the “little narratives” Lyotard valued so much can help: the stories of people who have walked a similar path and speak about it honestly.
addiction.practice: Name one area of life — a friendship, a walk, a craft — to which you would like to give back a little time. If you feel like it, you could listen to the stories of people who have walked a similar path, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: Lyotard’s essay “Rewriting Modernity” is about dealing with the past, and it suits the morning after surprisingly well. Heaviness, anxiety, shame and memory gaps are very uncomfortable, and they don’t make you a bad person. He distinguished two paths. You can try to reconstruct everything down to the last detail, frantically piecing together an exact chronology. Or you can, following Freud’s “working through,” patiently and unhurriedly let what matters surface on its own. Lyotard preferred the second. It follows that you don’t have to reconstruct the whole evening right now, in a state of anxiety, and pass sentence on yourself. Memory gaps are a “phrase” too — a silence that can’t be read yet. First you can take care of your body. And later, more calmly, see what really matters and whether you need to say something to someone.
hangover.practice: Postpone the “investigation” of last night for a couple of hours. For now, just step outside for five minutes of fresh air and let the past clear up on its own.

euphoria.text: Energy that can’t be put in the bank — that is one way to retell the “intensity” of Lyotard’s boldest book. A burst of euphoria, when everything seems possible, is a vivid experience, and you can enjoy it. In the early Libidinal Economy, Lyotard described affects as “intensities” — surges of energy that don’t accumulate, don’t turn into capital and don’t obey a plan. Later he himself looked at that book critically, but one of its thoughts remains valuable: an intensity is an event, not a possession. In other words, euphoria doesn’t have to be held on to, turned into proof or into an obligation for the future. It arrives as a “now” — the question “Is it happening?” to which the moment answers “yes.” To live it fully means accepting that it will end. That doesn’t make it any less real; it makes it an event rather than a debt.
euphoria.practice: Dance to one song however you like — not for a video, not for a purpose. Let the intensity pass through your body and dissipate, as it should.

crash.text: Music that has ended doesn’t become false because of it — Lyotard would agree. The drop after a high — after a celebration, a success, a vivid encounter — can be bitter, as if something had been taken away. In Libidinal Economy, Lyotard wrote that intensities by their nature do not accumulate: they flare up and dissipate. Later, in The Postmodern Condition, he showed how a society of “performativity” — of efficiency and constant results — expects continuous growth from us, as if the high should last forever. Lyotard might say that the “comedown” is the natural dissipation of an intensity, which looks like failure only against the demand to be in top form forever. You haven’t lost what happened: the event took place and remains an event. And the emptiness after it is not a verdict but an interval in which something new may happen, something you don’t yet expect.
crash.practice: Sit for a minute in the quiet after yesterday’s noise and listen to how an ordinary day sounds: the fridge, the street, your breath. That is music too — just quiet.

panic.text: In thinking about the sublime, Lyotard drew on Edmund Burke — a philosopher who wrote about terror as if he knew how it takes your breath away. A panic attack is genuinely frightening: your heart, your breathing, the sense that “something irreparable is about to happen.” Burke wrote that the strongest terror is the threat that nothing more will happen: that light, breath, connection with others will vanish. But the sublime, for Burke and Lyotard, arises when such a threat is held at a distance. It seems that panic is terror without distance, when the threat seems to be right inside your body. That is why whatever brings back even a little distance and a sense of “now” helps: something solid under you, your breath, the objects around you. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Each next breath is an answer to the question “Is it happening?”: yes, it is happening, you are here.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and breathe out more slowly than you breathe in. With each exhale note to yourself: “still happening” — the light, the floor, the breath go on.

dread.text: In four and a half billion years the Sun will die — Lyotard begins the essay “Can Thought Go On Without a Body?” with this thought, and there isn’t a drop of comforting lies in it. “What is the point of it all,” the sense of an abyss, is a heavy experience, and Lyotard looks straight at it. But what interests him is not despair but what this scale does to thought: it makes us value the body, memory, the very event of thinking. Another of his themes is the sublime, a mixture of pain and pleasure before what cannot be imagined. Lyotard would probably note that dread before the abyss and wonder that anything exists at all are two sides of the same feeling. The question “why” may never receive a final answer. But the fact that something happens rather than nothing is astonishing in itself, and you can stand on that.
dread.practice: Go out in the evening and find even one star in the sky, or just the glow of a streetlamp. Say to yourself: “And yet it is” — and stay with that for a minute.

fomo.text: Where is “the main thing” happening right now — at someone else’s party, on someone else’s trip? The feeling that everyone lives more interestingly while you’re in the wrong place is painful, and Lyotard would question the question itself: in the postmodern condition there is no single grand story explaining where the main thing is. Instead there are many “little narratives,” each with its own rules and values. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that the fear of missing out assumes that somewhere there is a centre, a real life you’ve been excluded from. But there is no centre — there are many places where something is happening. Lyotard wrote a great deal about the “now” — the event that happens here, before we manage to name it. The event isn’t taking place somewhere out there, with other people; it can begin in the very room where you are sitting.
fomo.practice: Name aloud one “little narrative” of your own from this week — a conversation, a walk, a song you found — that no one else has.

sleepless.text: Lyotard said thoughts are like clouds: they have no sharp edges, they drift and change shape. Insomnia is exhausting, and in the dark everything seems more hopeless than by day. In The Differend, Lyotard describes thinking as a chain of phrases in which each one calls for a continuation. At night this chain often locks into a single genre — the genre of the trial: accusation, defence, a new accusation, round and round. The other genres — care, humour, a friendly glance — seem to be asleep at night. It follows that night thoughts are not the final truth but one voice that sounds louder because the others have fallen silent. Lyotard valued the word “yet”: what cannot be resolved now may yet find its expression. Some questions can honestly be left until morning — not because they don’t matter, but because at night they lack anyone to talk to.
sleepless.practice: Lying in the dark, picture each nagging thought as a cloud: name it (“accusation-cloud,” “plan-cloud”) and let it drift past the edge of the window.

betrayal.text: Vows aren’t notarised — and Lyotard would explain why breaking them wounds more deeply than any broken contract. Betrayal destroys trust, and it feels as if the ground has been knocked out from under you. In The Differend, Lyotard distinguished “damage,” which can be proven and compensated, from a “wrong” (tort) — damage that has no way of being recognised. Betrayal often belongs to the second kind: you can’t “present” broken trust by rules the other person would accept. They have their language — “it just happened,” “I had my reasons” — and you have yours, and the two don’t translate into each other. In other words, your pain is testimony that a differend has occurred, even if no court will ever recognise it. It doesn’t have to be proven to be real. Lyotard urged us to seek new words for such wounds, and people able to hear them.
betrayal.practice: Tell one person who knows how to listen about the betrayal — not to reach a verdict, but so your pain is heard in at least one place.

jealousy.text: Lyotard was suspicious of the dream of total transparency — in society, in knowledge, between people. Jealousy, a burning mix of the fear of losing someone dear, pain and suspicion, dreams of exactly that. Lyotard insisted that every person has their own “idiom” — a way of speaking, feeling and linking their experience that can never be fully translated into someone else’s language. Even the person closest to you remains in some way untranslatable. Lyotard might say that jealousy often wants to translate the other completely — to know everything, understand everything, make their life transparent and subject to a single rule. But that is impossible even in the happiest love. Accepting that the other is not your “text” hurts, but it also frees you: you are not obliged to control the untranslatable. Instead, you can speak about your fear in your own language — directly and without accusation.
jealousy.practice: Recall one trait of the person you love that you still don’t understand, and let it remain a mystery — for today at least. Tell yourself: “The untranslatable is not a threat.”

resentment.text: Carrying for years a speech you were never allowed to give — that is how Lyotard might describe an old grudge. It can’t be let go of on command. Lyotard distinguished “litigation” — a dispute with shared rules, where a fair decision can be reached — from a “differend,” where the injured party has no language in which their damage will be recognised. It seems that resentment often lives so long precisely because it is an unrecognised differend. The wound has found neither a court nor a listener, and it keeps waiting. Lyotard didn’t say such wounds should simply be “forgotten.” He wrote that they need new ways of being expressed — new words, new listeners. Sometimes resentment eases not when the one who hurt you admits their guilt, but when you find a way to speak of it so that you are finally heard — by at least one person, or by yourself.
resentment.practice: Place a small stone in your palm and hold it, feeling the weight of the grudge. Then set it on the windowsill: don’t throw it away, just stop holding it.

heartbreak.text: Lyotard called our time an age when the grand stories have collapsed and meaning rests on small ones. A broken heart aches through the whole body: one of the most important small stories has collapsed. Lyotard wrote about “little narratives” — small stories that give life meaning. Love is one such story: it had its own words, jokes, rituals, a shared language. When a relationship ends, that story breaks off, and there is no longer anyone to answer in the old language. Lyotard stressed that after every phrase there will necessarily be a next one, but what it will be is not determined in advance. Lyotard would probably note that the end of a relationship is not the end of your story but a point after which it will inevitably continue, even if it’s hard to imagine how right now. There’s no need to rush the next chapter. Grieving is also a way of continuing the phrase.
heartbreak.practice: Imagine your story as a book in which this chapter has ended but there are more pages. Think of a title for the next chapter — even a single word.

impostor.text: Lyotard’s most famous book, The Postmodern Condition, was a commissioned report on knowledge for the government of Quebec — and in it he asked who has the right to count as knowing at all. The fear of being exposed any moment is agonising, and it comes even to highly competent people. Lyotard showed that the old grand justifications of knowledge — like “the progress of reason” — have lost their force, and today legitimacy rests mainly on “performativity”: on what works. No one possesses a final “certificate” of their authenticity anymore. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that you are not the only one who can’t produce absolute proof of your right to be here — no one has such proof. You are not a fraud among genuine experts; everyone around you is learning, making mistakes and getting by on the fact that their work sometimes comes off.
impostor.practice: Recall one thing you did well without any instructions. Say aloud to yourself: “Here is my justification — it is in what I did.”

self_hatred.text: A judge, a prosecutor and no defence lawyer — that is often the inner critic’s court, and Lyotard, thinker of unjust trials, would recognise it. When the critic insists you are bad, a failure, “not right,” it hurts — and its verdict is not the truth about you. In Lectures d’enfance (Readings of Infancy, 1991), Lyotard wrote about “infancy” (from the Latin infantia, “not speaking”) as the part of a person that cannot explain itself, justify itself, give an account. It is there in each of us all our lives. For Lyotard this is not a flaw but the very thing that is human and cannot be reduced to efficiency or calculation. It follows that the inner critic demands that this fragile, imperfect part of you give an account of itself by someone else’s rules. But it isn’t supposed to be able to. It cannot be condemned in a language it doesn’t speak. Tenderness toward it is justice.
self_hatred.practice: Put a hand on your cheek, the way someone once comforted you as a child, and say quietly: “You don’t have to justify yourself.” Keep your hand there for a minute.

helplessness.text: A train without a driver, picking up speed — that is one way to picture “development” in Lyotard’s The Inhuman: a process of optimisation that moves on its own, barely consulting people. Being powerless to change something is hard to bear, especially when you are trying very hard. He admits honestly that an individual often cannot stand up to this process. In other words, your helplessness is in large part an accurate perception of scale, not a personal failure. But Lyotard also speaks of another “inhuman” — an unmanageable, living part of us that is still capable of being touched and of responding. Even when little depends on you, you keep the ability to choose how to answer life’s next phrase: to notice, to speak, to disagree. It isn’t much, but it isn’t nothing.
helplessness.practice: Do one small thing that is entirely in your power: water a plant, thank someone, make the bed. Say: “This is mine.”

procrastination.text: The blank canvas frightened even great painters, and Lyotard saw that fear as reverence for the event. When you can’t get started even though you really need to, it’s easy to suspect yourself of laziness. Reflecting on artists like Barnett Newman, Lyotard wrote about the anxious question “Is it happening?” that stands before every beginning — before a blank canvas or an empty page. A beginning is an event that can’t be fully planned in advance. Lyotard might say that procrastination is sometimes not laziness but trepidation before that open “now,” where nothing has been decided yet. What’s more, in a world of “performativity,” every beginning seems obliged to become a result at once, which is even more frightening. If you relieve the first step of the obligation to be good, starting becomes easier. Lyotard valued the uncertain, searching beginning — that is exactly where the new is born.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and make the first “brushstroke” — one sentence, one line of code, one washed plate. Don’t decide in advance what comes next.

uprooted.text: Lyotard taught in Algeria in the early 1950s and knew life between two languages firsthand. Being cut off from home can go very deep: language, habits, the very ground slip away. Lyotard wrote a great deal about the incommensurability of languages and “language games”: what is weighty and clear in one language may sound hollow, or not sound at all, in another. Emigration is life at the junction of such games, where many of your phrases lose weight in translation. It seems that the pain of uprootedness is not a failure to adapt but an honest experience of a differend between two worlds. Lyotard didn’t demand that you choose one language and give up the other. He valued the ability to live with the incommensurable without reducing it to a common denominator. Your doubleness is not a mistake but a particular knowledge that those who never left don’t have.
uprooted.practice: Say aloud one word from your native language that has no exact translation, and stay with its sound for a minute. This is your idiom — it can’t be lost in a move.

quote.text: Postmodern knowledge is not simply a tool of the authorities; it refines our sensitivity to differences and reinforces our ability to tolerate the incommensurable.
quote.author: Jean-François Lyotard

overload.text: In 1979, when a personal computer was still a curiosity, Lyotard predicted the “computerisation of society”: knowledge would turn into information — a commodity produced, sold and consumed for the sake of efficiency. Overload from the endless feed, notifications and news is exhausting, and it is not your inability to “keep up.” Later, in The Inhuman, he wrote about constant acceleration demanding ever more speed and memory from people. Lyotard would probably note that overload is a collision between the human body with its rhythm and a system running at inhuman speed. Your body doesn’t have to keep pace with it. Lyotard valued the slowness of writing, thinking, contemplating — what doesn’t fit into the flow of information. Slowing down is not falling behind but returning to a human tempo.
overload.practice: Switch off all screens for five minutes and listen to how the room sounds. In that pause, let your body return to its own, human tempo.

unreality.text: Your palm touches the table before you have time to think about it — Lyotard loved such tiny head starts. The sense that the world, or you yourself, is not quite real can be frightening and disorienting. Lyotard thought a great deal about how we experience an event. He wrote that an event always happens before consciousness manages to grasp it: first “it happens,” and only afterwards do we understand what. Between what occurred and making sense of it there is a gap. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that the feeling of unreality is as if this gap has stretched — the world goes on, while the sense that “I am here, this is happening to me” lags behind. That doesn’t mean the world has vanished. Lyotard valued the smallest sensations — a sound, a colour, a touch — which, in his words, awaken the “minimal soul.” They can be a good bridge back to the “now.”
unreality.practice: Put both palms on a table and press, feeling its hardness and coolness. Name aloud three sounds around you — let understanding catch up with the event.

awe.text: “The sublime is now,” wrote the painter Barnett Newman, and Lyotard made the phrase almost a motto. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling. For Lyotard it is perhaps the central experience: he called it “the sublime” and devoted to it his book Lessons on the Analytic of the Sublime and the famous essay “The Sublime and the Avant-Garde.” Following Kant, he described the sublime as a mixture of pleasure and pain: we encounter something the imagination cannot hold — the ocean, the starry sky, a huge painting — and feel at once our own smallness and elation. From Lyotard’s point of view, this feeling bears witness to the unpresentable — to the fact that the world is bigger than any image of it. Awe doesn’t need to be explained or photographed. You can simply live it as an event, as an answer to the question “Is it happening?” to which your whole body answers “yes.”
awe.practice: Go to the largest open space nearby — the sky over the rooftops, a river, a field — and look in silence for a minute, without trying to describe it.

relief.text: When a storm passes you by, you exhale with a special feeling that Edmund Burke called “delight” and Lyotard took up in thinking about the sublime: the pleasure that arises when a threat recedes. Relief is a warm feeling, worth savouring. It isn’t ordinary joy but relief after fear, mixed with amazement at still being here. In other words, relief is an event, the moment when the question “Will anything else happen?” receives the answer “yes, life goes on.” It shows how much strength was going into waiting for disaster. Relief doesn’t have to be turned straight into a new task. You can let your body feel this delight — and remember it as a sign that a threat can recede.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and feel where your body has let go — shoulders, jaw, belly. Put a palm there and say: “Life goes on.”

calm.text: Morning and evening, the turning seasons, a kettle put on at the same time every day — in “Domus and the Megalopolis” Lyotard called this everyday rhythm “home” (Latin domus) and saw a quiet wisdom in it. Calm and peace are infrequent guests, and it is good to cherish them. This rhythm, he said, is increasingly being pushed out by the speed of the megalopolis. Lyotard might say that calm is the moment you fall back into such a domestic rhythm, where nothing needs to be sped up or proven. It is not a result and does not serve efficiency. That is exactly why it is valuable in itself. Let calm last without asking what it is for.
calm.practice: Do one familiar household task — brew tea, fold laundry — at its natural pace, speeding nothing up. Listen to the rhythm of “home.”

inspiration.text: Lyotard might begin with a question: what if the rules appear only after you take the first step? Inspiration is a joyful feeling, when something new seems to be striving to appear on its own. Lyotard linked it with “paralogy” — the search for the new through disagreement with familiar rules. He wrote that the postmodern artist and writer work without rules given in advance: the rules of what they are doing become visible only afterwards, once the work is done. It seems that inspiration is the moment when you act without yet knowing the rules, and that is not a mistake but the condition of creativity. There’s no need to test the idea for efficiency or “correctness” right away. The question “Is it happening?” rings especially bright here: something is being born, and it isn’t yet known what. You can simply enjoy this moment.
inspiration.practice: In two minutes, draw something with no plan — a line, a blot, a shape — and only afterwards ask what rules it followed.

schadenfreude.text: Lyotard would describe even a dinner conversation as a match in which every remark is a move. A secret pleasure at someone else’s failure is familiar to almost everyone and doesn’t make you a bad person: in The Postmodern Condition Lyotard writes that to speak is in some sense to compete — to make moves, to win and to lose. He called this “agonistics” (from the Greek agon, contest). Lyotard would probably note that schadenfreude is born where life turns into one continuous competition: someone else’s loss seems for a moment to be your win. It happens easily in a world where everything is compared and ranked. But Lyotard also stressed something else: there are many games, and most of them have no shared score. Someone’s failure in one game adds nothing to your life and takes nothing from it. You can notice this flash and not continue the game.
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine that you and this person are playing not against each other but on the same team — against boredom. What move would you make now?

contempt.text: “Incredulity toward metanarratives” — that is how Lyotard defined the postmodern: toward grand stories that explain everything and put everyone in their place — who is progressive and who is backward, who is “right” and who is not. Contempt, a cold “looking-down” feeling, often protects something vulnerable. Such stories granted the right to look down on others. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that contempt often leans on a grand narrative of this kind — about how “normal” people are supposed to live — and borrows its sense of being right from it. If you start to doubt that narrative, you discover that in front of you is simply another person with their own “little story.” You don’t have to love or approve of them. But perhaps you can decline the role of judge that the grand narrative offers you.
contempt.practice: Ask yourself: from which “grand story” am I looking down on this person? For a minute, try hearing their little narrative — how they would tell their own life.

disgust.text: Your face wrinkles before you have time to think — Lyotard would call this a judgement without criteria. Disgust is an instant, almost bodily “no,” and there is nothing shameful in it. In the dialogue-book Just Gaming (Au juste), Lyotard talks a lot about how we constantly “judge without criteria”: we evaluate without a ready-made rule, feeling our way, as it were. Following Kant, he saw such judgement as a normal part of life, not a mistake. It follows that disgust is exactly this kind of quick judgement without criteria: the body says “no” before the mind finds a reason. This judgement deserves respect: it is signalling something. But Lyotard also stressed that every judgement without criteria has to be tested anew each time. Disgust toward a person, or toward yourself, is an opening remark, not a final verdict.
disgust.practice: Step back from whatever disgusted you and take three slow breaths. Then ask yourself: “What exactly did my body say ‘no’ to — and does my mind have to agree?”

revenge.text: Imagine filing a complaint and finding the window closed forever — Lyotard described exactly such situations. The wish for revenge tells you that you have been hurt, and that the hurt demands recognition. In The Differend, Lyotard distinguishes two kinds of harm. “Damage” (dommage) can be proven and compensated by shared rules — in a court, for example. A “wrong” (tort) is harm that also strips the injured party of the means to prove it: there are no witnesses, no fitting words, no court that would listen. In other words, the thirst for revenge is especially strong when there is a wrong: when there is neither recognition nor a way to speak of it, what remains is the fantasy of taking justice into your own hands. But revenge doesn’t give you a voice — it only adds a new harm. What matters more is finding where, and to whom, you can tell what happened: a friend, a diary, someone who knows how to listen.
revenge.practice: Write down what happened to you as if you were telling it to an honest witness. Who in your life could listen to this story?

anger_at_loved.text: Lyotard wrote about feelings as a current running through the body: a current can’t be cancelled, only directed somewhere. Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can flare up especially strongly, and afterwards you feel ashamed of it. In Libidinal Economy, Lyotard describes feelings as “intensities” — energy flowing through the body. Society, family and roles are “dispositifs,” devices that channel this energy into prescribed courses: to care, to endure, to be a good parent or child. But energy never fits into those channels completely. Lyotard might say that anger at someone you love is often a breakthrough of energy that a role has held back for a long time. It doesn’t mean love has vanished; it means you are more than your role. Anger gives no right to wound, but it can show you where a role has become too tight.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises, give the energy a safe outlet: walk briskly up and down the stairs or clench and unclench your fists ten times. Then say one sentence as yourself, not as your role.

ambivalence.text: Mountains that take your breath away and frighten you at once — Lyotard knew that two opposite feelings can live in a single instant. Loving a person while being unable to stand them is hard and confusing, but it is a very human state. Lyotard reflected a great deal on “the sublime” — a feeling which, following Kant, he described as a mixture of pleasure and pain, attraction and terror at once. For him this feeling is not a contradiction to be eliminated but a sign of meeting something larger than our familiar categories. It seems that mixed feelings toward someone close are relatives of the sublime: the person is too large and complex to fit into a single emotion. Love and the unbearable live side by side because this person touches you deeply. There’s no need to hurry toward a synthesis. Ambivalence is not a mistake but a testimony to how much someone matters.
ambivalence.practice: Picture this person very far away, like a mountain on the horizon, and then very close. Notice how the mix of your feelings changes at each distance.

guilty_relief.text: For Lyotard every person has their own “idiom” of feeling that can’t be retold in ready-made words. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: “how can I feel this?” Relief and love can exist together. Lyotard urged us to be incredulous toward “metanarratives” — grand stories that prescribe to everyone how life should be understood. Loss has such a grand story too: “someone who truly loves feels nothing but grief.” Lyotard would probably note that shame over relief is the result of this narrative’s pressure. Your situation is a “little narrative,” a story of its own: long caregiving, exhausting worry, conflicts that have finally ended. In such a story, relief is natural and does not cancel love. Your feeling doesn’t have to obey a general script in order to be honest.
guilty_relief.practice: Quietly tell yourself both truths at once: “I feel lighter” and “It hurts.” Breathe with them for a minute, without choosing which one matters more.

indifference.text: Skin rubbed for too long stops feeling — Lyotard would say the soul works in a similar way. Sometimes you aren’t moved by what you “should” be moved by — and guilt arrives. In The Inhuman, Lyotard uses the word “passibility” — the capacity to be affected, to receive, to let something happen to you. He considered it the most fragile and precious human quality. And he noticed that modern life, with its speed and demand for efficiency, depletes this capacity: being affected takes time and slowness. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that your indifference is not coldness but perhaps an exhaustion of passibility. It can’t be switched on by order. It can only be looked after: by giving yourself pauses, slowness, quiet. Then the ability to respond will gradually return on its own.
indifference.practice: Demand nothing of yourself for ten minutes: sit by a window and let the world touch you however faintly. Passibility doesn’t return on command.

escape.text: A boat that has left the shore and hasn’t yet chosen a course — Lyotard loved this state and even put the word “drift” into a book title. The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your role — tells you that your current life has become too tight, and it is a legitimate signal. One of Lyotard’s early books is called Drifting Away from Marx and Freud (Dérive à partir de Marx et Freud). He chose the word “drift” deliberately: not a revolutionary break and not flight, but a gradual, free shifting, when you allow the current to carry you out of familiar places. Lyotard saw drift as a way of thinking and living without submitting to a single system. It follows that the pull to escape is the voice of this drift. It doesn’t necessarily demand an abrupt break. You can start drifting: shift little by little, try new things, loosen the tether to what has become too tight, and see where the current takes you.
escape.practice: Make one small shift today: walk home a different way or sit in a different seat. Notice how drift begins with a couple of steps aside.

forbidden_attraction.text: A wave doesn’t ask permission where to roll — that is how Lyotard thought of desire in Libidinal Economy. An attraction that is “not allowed” — to someone unavailable or “wrong” — can be embarrassing and frightening. But a feeling is not an action. In Libidinal Economy, Lyotard described desire not as lack but as an “intensity” — a flow of energy that obeys neither morality nor logic. He argued against theories that see in every desire a “hidden truth” about a person. For Lyotard, an intensity simply happens, like a wave, and doesn’t have to mean anything. In other words, a forbidden attraction is such a wave: it doesn’t choose where to flow, and it is not a command. You can feel it, acknowledge its strength, and not hurry either to interpret it or to decide anything. A wave doesn’t have to become an action to be acknowledged.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Watch the attraction like a wave: where it rises in your body, where it crests, how it falls. Just watch, without jumping in.

social_anxiety.text: Lyotard would suggest seeing any conversation as a network rather than a stage: there is no audience in it, only nodes passing messages to one another. Fear of people and their judgement is exhausting: every meeting feels like an exam. In The Postmodern Condition, Lyotard writes that the self is never an island: each of us is a node in a fabric of relations through which messages, questions and answers pass. He adds that even the least noticeable person is always located at some point in this network — both receiving and passing things on. Lyotard might say that social anxiety often paints a picture in which you are a lone examinee and everyone around you is the examining board. But in fact you are a player in a shared game where everyone has their own move and everyone is a little nervous. You don’t need to win the conversation. It is enough to make your move — a question, a remark, a smile — and let others make theirs.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, simply pass one thing along: good news, a link, a question. You are not an examinee — you are a node something passes through.

uncertainty.text: How long is the coast of Brittany? Following Mandelbrot, Lyotard noted that the more precisely you measure it, the longer it gets. Uncertainty is hard: it isn’t clear what will happen, and you long for something to hold on to. The Postmodern Condition has a chapter on “postmodern science.” Lyotard writes that modern science increasingly studies not stable laws but instabilities: catastrophes, fractals, paradoxes, unpredictable leaps. For it, unpredictability is not a failure of knowledge but its new subject. It seems that the uncertainty in your life is not a sign that you have missed something. The world at every level is arranged so that exact prediction is often impossible. That is unsettling, but it is also where there is room for the new and unexpected. You don’t have to wait for complete clarity; you can explore the situation with the curiosity of a scientist studying instability.
uncertainty.practice: Look at a tree branch or a crack in the asphalt and trace its bends for a minute. Notice: the unpredictable can also be beautiful and steady.

waiting.text: An alarm that hasn’t rung yet, a letter that hasn’t arrived yet — waiting for results, a reply or news lives only in the future. Lyotard would offer an antidote taken from painting. Lyotard wrote the essay “Newman: The Instant” about the painter Barnett Newman, who gave his paintings titles like Here, Now, Be. Lyotard admired how these paintings return the viewer to the present instant: not to the past or an anticipated future, but to the “now” that is happening right before your eyes. Lyotard would probably note that waiting carries you off into the future, and the present seems to stop existing. But the “now” keeps happening even while you wait. You can notice it: the light in the room, a sound, your breath. The waiting won’t disappear, but life will appear beside it again.
waiting.practice: Stand before any single-coloured surface — a wall, the sky, a door — and simply look at the colour for a minute. Say to yourself: “Here. Now.”

regret.text: A stuck record or a manuscript being rewritten — in “Rewriting Modernity” Lyotard, drawing on Freud, distinguishes exactly these two ways of dealing with the past. Regret over something you did or didn’t do can come back again and again. You can endlessly repeat it, replaying the same thing. Or you can “work it through”: return to the past freely, as in free association, letting what was previously invisible come through. Lyotard called this kind of working through “anamnesis” — recollection. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that regret often gets stuck in repetition mode: “if only I had…”. But it can be shifted into working-through mode: not judging the past again, but listening to what it may still have to say. Then regret stops being a verdict and becomes a source of understanding.
regret.practice: Retell that story aloud once — but the way you would tell it to a kind friend ten years from now. What changed in the tone?

longing.text: “A tall man with a warm voice” could be anyone, but a name points to only one. You can long for a particular person almost physically — it is precisely them you miss, not someone similar — and in The Differend Lyotard reflects a great deal on proper names. He writes that a name is not a description that can be swapped for another: it points “rigidly” to one single person, and around it gathers a whole world of phrases, memories, stories. It follows that longing is a feeling that answers to a name: behind it stands a world that can’t be translated into any other name. That is why consolations like “there will be others” help so little. Your longing speaks of this person’s uniqueness. You can honour it: say the name, recall the phrases connected with them.
longing.practice: Say this person’s name quietly and listen to the world that rises around it: a voice, a place, a joke. Stay in that world for a minute.

world_pain.text: Lyotard believed that sometimes all that remains to a person is to be a witness, even when nothing can be fixed. Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can weigh you down, and it speaks of your sensitivity. In The Differend, reflecting on the catastrophes of the twentieth century, Lyotard compares them to an earthquake so powerful that it destroyed the very instruments that could have measured it. All that remains is feeling — and Lyotard insists that this feeling must be respected: it bears witness to something for which we don’t yet have words. In other words, your pain for the world is also testimony. It is not useless or “excessive.” But testimony needs a voice, not endless accumulation. You can express this pain — in words, in taking part, in offering support — instead of carrying it silently on your own.
world_pain.practice: Tell one person close to you, in two or three sentences, what exactly hurts you in what is happening, and ask them just to listen. Testimony shared with someone is easier to carry.

rejection.text: A chess player isn’t taken onto a football team not because they’re a bad player — it’s simply a different game, Lyotard would say. Rejection wounds painfully: it feels as if you have been judged not enough. In The Postmodern Condition, Lyotard writes about “legitimation” — how, in different “language games,” it is decided what counts as right, valuable, suitable. Each game has its own rules, and there is no single supreme game that judges all the others. Lyotard might say that a rejection is a decision made within one particular game, by its rules: this company, this person, this situation. It is not a universal verdict on your worth. In another game, with other rules, the very same thing in you may turn out to be exactly what is needed. The pain of rejection is real, but it speaks of a mismatch, not of your being “not enough” in general.
rejection.practice: Name aloud one “game” in which you are valued: a friendship, a craft, your family, some skill. Say: “There, my moves count.”

abandonment.text: For a baby, an adult leaving the room is a whole catastrophe: they don’t yet know the adult will come back, and they can’t say anything. The fear of being abandoned is exhausting — you catch every sign of someone drawing away — and, grown from old wounds, it deserves gentleness. In The Inhuman and in Lectures d’enfance (Readings of Infancy), Lyotard reflects on childhood using the Latin infantia — “not speaking.” A human being is born helpless, unable to survive without another, and this original dependence never disappears; it stays in us. It seems that the fear of abandonment is the voice of that infancy in us, a memory of a time when another’s leaving really was a threat. Now you are an adult with your own supports, but infancy keeps speaking. There is no need to be ashamed of it. You can treat this fear the way you would treat a frightened child: gently, without mockery.
abandonment.practice: Wrap your arms around yourself, the way you would hold a little one, and say quietly: “I’m here, I won’t leave.” Stay like that for a minute.

unrequited.text: A letter that got no reply was still written, and read — by you, at least. Unrequited love wounds painfully: you reach out to someone and there is no answer, and Lyotard would suggest looking at this through the structure of the phrase itself. In The Differend, Lyotard describes the “universe of a phrase”: it contains the one who speaks, the one addressed, what is spoken about, and the sense. Every phrase, even one left unanswered, has already happened and has already created its own small world. Lyotard would probably note that your love is such a phrase. The place of the one who should answer stands empty, and that hurts. But the phrase itself is real: the feeling was there, you lived it, and it said a great deal about you. Lyotard stressed that another phrase always follows, but which one is not decided in advance. The next phrase of your life may be addressed to someone else — including yourself.
unrequited.practice: Take a five-minute walk and silently address your feeling to the sky, the trees, the street — to the world rather than to one person. Notice that a phrase doesn’t vanish without an answer.

humiliation.text: All his life Lyotard defended the right to the next move — the right to answer, even when someone wants to silence you. Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you had been stripped of your voice and put on display. In The Postmodern Condition, Lyotard defines “terror” as a way of winning by excluding the other from the game, or threatening to: not out-arguing them, but forcing them into silence. Take Lyotard’s thought one step further, and it turns out that humiliation is a small instance of such terror: someone tries to put you out of the game, deny you the right to a move, make you a “nobody.” But this speaks of the other person’s methods, not of your worth. Humiliation works as long as you accept the exclusion as the truth. Taking back your move means speaking again: telling what happened to someone who will listen, writing down your version, returning to the games where you are respected.
humiliation.practice: Stand up straight, plant your feet firmly and say aloud a calm sentence you weren’t allowed to say then. Your move isn’t cancelled — only postponed.

body_shame.text: Engineers dream of transferring the mind into a computer and doing without a body — Lyotard regarded this dream with deep suspicion. Dissatisfaction with your body can be quiet and constant, and it deserves care rather than more criticism. The Inhuman contains the essay “Can Thought Go On Without a Body?”. Lyotard’s answer is no. Thought, feeling, memory, desire — all of it happens in the body and thanks to the body. The body is not a shell to be improved but the condition of your being able to think, love and notice the world at all. It follows that body shame treats the body as an object to be assessed from outside, whereas the body is your way of being. You are not the “owner” of a defective object but a living being who thinks and feels with your body. You can shift your attention from how your body looks to what it makes possible.
body_shame.practice: Make three slow movements — stretch, turn your head, wiggle your fingers — and notice not how your body looks but what it lets you feel and think.

illness.text: What is left to the soul when the body is ill? Lyotard would answer: the smallest touches of the world. When the body lets you down, it is hard both physically and emotionally: plans collapse, the world shrinks to symptoms. In Postmodern Fables, Lyotard wrote the essay “Anima Minima” — about the “minimal soul.” He believed the soul awakens when something touches it: a colour, a sound, a smell. Without these touches, he says, the soul seems to fall asleep. In other words, during illness the world of sensations often narrows to pain and discomfort, and the soul lacks other touches. That is why the small good sensations that remain available matter so much: the taste of tea, light in the window, a familiar voice, the softness of a blanket. They don’t cure, but they gently sustain the soul while the body goes through something hard.
illness.practice: Choose one pleasant sensation available to you now: a taste, a sound, light, a touch. Stay with it for a minute.

pride.text: The first person to walk an unknown trail couldn’t consult a guidebook — Lyotard valued such steps above any instructions. Pride in something you have done is a healthy, well-earned feeling, worth living through without embarrassment. In the essay “Answering the Question: What Is Postmodernism?” Lyotard writes about artists and writers who work without ready-made rules: the rules of what they have made become clear only afterwards. He described this with the tense of the “future anterior” — what “will have been done.” Lyotard might say that pride is especially deserved when you have done something for which there was no instruction: found your own way, taken a risk, invented something. What you did sets a rule that didn’t exist before. That is worth noticing and celebrating without comparing it to other people’s yardsticks: you yourself created the measure of your act.
pride.practice: Tell someone how you did it: where there were no instructions and what you came up with yourself. Allow yourself not to play it down.

quote.text: The artist and the writer, then, are working without rules in order to formulate the rules of what will have been done.
quote.author: Jean-François Lyotard
quote.source: Answering the Question: What Is Postmodernism? (1982)

melancholy.text: Lyotard loved art that longs for what cannot be shown — and still offers the consolation of form. Bittersweet sadness is a quiet, tender feeling in which there is no misfortune, only attention to what is gone and fragile. In the essay “Answering the Question: What Is Postmodernism?” Lyotard distinguishes two moods in art. One he calls “melancholia”: art longs for the unattainable and consoles with beautiful form. The other is “novatio”: joyful experiment with the unknown. Lyotard didn’t mock melancholia — he saw it as one legitimate way of relating to what cannot be held on to. It seems that bittersweet sadness is your personal experience of such melancholia: a longing for the unattainable, warmed by the beauty of form — music, autumn light, a memory. You can live through it without hurrying on to “novatio.” Melancholy knows how to console too.
melancholy.practice: Put on one slow piece of music and listen to it all the way through, looking out of the window. Let the sadness rest in a beautiful form — it is at home there.
